message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe.  
Below is a concise overview of its key physical, chemical, and practical properties.

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Symbol | H |
| | Group | 1 (alkali metals) – though it behaves as a non‑metal |
| | Period | 1 |
| | Block | s |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Valence electrons | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Isotopes | Protium (¹H, 99.98 %), Deuterium (²H, 0.02 %) – stable; Tritium (³H) – radioactive |
| **Physical Properties** | State at STP | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density (STP) | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0000899 g cm⁻³) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14 K) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| | Specific heat capacity | 14.304 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 25 °C) |
| | Ionization energy | 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ (first) |
| | Electron affinity | 72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Molar volume (ideal gas) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Bond type | Covalent (H₂) |
| | Diatomic molecule | H₂ |
| | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive in air (range 4–75 % H₂ in air) |
| | Reactivity | Forms hydrides with metals; reacts with halogens (e.g., H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl) |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a weak acid in aqueous solution (hydronium formation) |
| | Basic behavior | Acts as a weak base (forming hydride ions, e.g., NaH + H₂O → NaOH + H₂) |
| | Hydrogen bonding | H atoms can participate in hydrogen bonds when bonded to electronegative atoms (e.g., in water, alcohols) |
| | Redox behavior | Strong reducing agent (e.g., H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O) |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Most common, stable |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, heavier isotope (used in D₂O “heavy water”) |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (half‑life ≈12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion research |
| **Practical Uses** | Fuel | Rocket propellant (liquid H₂ + liquid O₂) |
| | Energy | Hydrogen fuel cells (electrochemical conversion to electricity) |
| | Industry | Ammonia synthesis (Haber process), petroleum refining (hydrocracking), methanol production, hydrogenation reactions |
| | Research | Tracer studies, NMR spectroscopy (¹H NMR), neutron scattering |
| | Medicine | MRI contrast agents (deuterated compounds) |
| | Food & Beverage | Baking (leavening agents), beverage carbonation (CO₂/H₂ mixtures) |
| **Safety & Handling** | Explosive limits | Lower explosive limit (LEL) ≈4 %, upper explosive limit (UEL) ≈75 % in air |
| | Storage | Requires cryogenic tanks (liquid H₂) or high‑pressure cylinders (gas) |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but inhalation of high concentrations can cause hypoxia (oxygen displacement) |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Hydrogen’s low mass makes it ideal for balloons, lift gases, and as a benchmark in physics experiments.
- **Highly reactive**: Its single valence electron drives many industrial processes, from ammonia synthesis to fuel cells.
- **Versatile isotopes**: Deuterium and tritium enable specialized applications such as heavy‑water reactors and fusion research.
- **Energy carrier**: Hydrogen is central to the emerging hydrogen economy, offering clean combustion and efficient storage options.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
